div.head: The Argument.
div.p: Agamemnon, having confided the guardianship of his kingdom to Ægisthus during his absence at the siege of Troy, returns to resume his sovereignty. His wife, Clytemnestra, conspires with Ægisthus, for whom she has conceived a passion, and they, lying in wait for the king as he is leaving the bath, barbarously slay him with an axe (an-acc-ident which possibly anticipated for him his Homeric title Αν-αξ ἀνδρων ᾿Αγαμέμνων.) The guilty parties are married, and Ægisthus usurps the throne of Argos, to the exclusion of the rightful heir, Orestes. Electra, however, true to her father's cause, and fearful for the safety of her brother, sends him away privately to the court of his uncle Strophius, king of Phocis, until he shall be of years to avenge their father's death, and claim his rights. Seven years elapse, at the expiration of which, indeed, on the anniversary of the marriage of Ægisthus, the present drama opens. The people are crushed beneath the despotic sway of Ægisthus, who, in his turn, bows in slavish submission to the will of his strong-minded lady, while both combine to render wretched the life of Electra. She, unswerving in her loyalty to her father's cause, is awaiting the expected return of Orestes, who, having spread a report of his own death at a chariot race, the more easily to gain admission to the palace, arrives with his friend Pylades at Mycenæ;-they have provided themselves with a funeral urn, supposed to contain the ashes of Orestes, to give additional probability to their story—they are hospitably received, as the bearers of welcome tidings. Orestes then discloses himself, but is spared the personal infliction of vengeance on the usurpers by the intervention of Nemesis, who contrives that they themselves are made the instruments of their own destruction.

div.head: Scene First.—Hall of Audience in the Palace of Ægisthus —through the columns at back, a view of the City of Mycenae.
div.stage: Ægisthus discovered seated on his throne, surrounded by Courtiers. A Procession appears, L. U. E. from behind the columns, bearing costly gifts, and enters C. to the following

sp.l: On this auspicious day, great king,
Our homes we all forsake
Thus freely at your feet to fling
What else your hand would take.
These tributes to your sovereign sway
Vouchsafe, sire, to accept,
For loyalty must give away
What prudence would have kept;
'Tis thus we come to pay our court,
Though traitors' lips may say
The privilege is dearly bought
When there's so much to pay.

sp.speaker: Courtiers
sp.l: Long live the King!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: With gratitude we take your generous proffers,
Yet, 'ere we can dismiss them to our coffers,
Be sure the precious gifts upon us pressed,
Have touched our heart before they reach our chest!
'Tis, as 'tis obvious you are all aware,
Both by your presence here, and presents there,
The anniversary of that happy day
When Clytemnestra gave her hand away,
Threw me the reins of government, indeed,
For, from our bridal I've reigned in her stead.

sp.speaker: Philar.
sp.l: We trust no anniversaries, dread sovereign,
Less happy round the royal head are hovering.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: A cordial wish in which we sympathise,
And hope we mayn't see any worse arise.
Meantime proclaim a general holiday,
That all may give their loyal feelings play
By general joy in every direction—
In one outburst of unrestrained affection.

sp.speaker: Philar.
sp.l: Pardon, dread king, you've made a slight mistake
We fear the vulgar rabble scarce partake
The loyal sentiments which animate us
But, rather—

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Yes we know, they rather hate us

sp.speaker: Philar.
sp.l: Sire, Agamemnon, it must be confessed, is,
With aching hearts remembered, and Orestes
Whom, if he should return, they swear they'll make King.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: These aching hearts shall find their head is a-king!

div.stage: Enter one of Clytemnestra's Ladies, L.

sp.speaker: Lady
sp.l: Most gracious sovereign—

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: (starting up angrily) How now? What means this insolent intrusion?

sp.speaker: Lady
sp.l: Sire, the queen's
Desirous you'll be good enough to say
If you mean to sit preaching there all day—
Because, when you have nothing else to do
She would be glad to have a word with you.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: (with change of manner) The playful dear! how quaintly she reveals
The jealousy she of our absence feels!
But she's so fond of us we must excuse her,
Besides there's nought in life we can refuse her.

div.stage: Exit Lady, L.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: (aside) At least a long experience tells me so,
(aloud) All which considered, p'r'aps you'd better go

div.stage: (chorus repeated—Procession goes off, R. U. E.—Courtiers exeunt, L. U. E.)
Enter Clytemnestra, L.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: (with change of manner) Oh! so they've left you?
I thought you'd company—pray what's bereft you
Of common sense, (you'd not too much to start with
Certainly, none you could afford to part with,)
That these last three nights you have left your bed
To indulge in restless wanderings over head?

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Though my arising may to you seem queer,
Your own horizon's anything but clear,
The seeds of revolution, taking root,
Promise to both of us an early shoot;
Our cutting off their late king with a hatchet,
Returning from the bath, the rebels snatch at
As cause against us——and exclaim, in wrath,
He got his head shaved when he went to Bath!

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: With honeyed words, I have disguised the facts.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Words won't avail, they'll judge us by our axe;
In nightly visions, Agamemnon's shade
Calls on his son for vengeance!

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: What! afraid
Of a night phantom?

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: I don't mean a pun,
"Tis not the shade I fear it is the son!
And there's the daughter too—the girl, Electra—
I always pop on when I least expect her
Laden with curses, every sort and size
For application to my head and eyes;
I wish, unless her language she can soften,
That peerless orphan would appear less often.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Broken of that, she soon to us will bend herself.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: She may be broken, but will never mend herself;
Besides, her dress is—where got I can't tell,
Apparel quite without a parallel :
Wherein she wanders forth at early morn,
Unkempt, uncinctured, with her stockings torn,
In her hand offerings, in her eye a tear
To imbrue her father's lamen-table beer.
Chrysothemis is of another sort,
On politics she never wastes a thought.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: I doubt if she's a thought to waste, unless
It be upon the fashion of her dress.
Thus different ways, each in her duty flags,
One's over dressed, the other done to rags.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Chrysothemis I'm sure is worth a dozen
Of her pale, slipshod, sentimental cousin.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: A worthless minx!

div.stage: (Chrysothemis is heard singing without)

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Hark! here's the dear child coming,
An opera tune most opera-tunely humming;
You called her worthless, and you were not wrong,
Since she is going now for an old song.

div.stage: Enter Chrysothemis, R. U. E. down C., a bunch of violets in her hand, singing and dancing.

spGrp.head: Air, "By the margin of fair Zurich's Waters."

sp.l: As the morning looked fair in all quarters,
And I knew
A bank where these lie-a-beds lay,
These the fairest of fair Nature's daughters
That on it grew,
I gathered and brought them away!
And you'll own no one bolder can be,
For it don't with my practice agree
To rise at this time of the day;
Aye, aye, you
May stare—but the duty to pay
I owe you I owe you on this happy day,
I owe you I owe you drove all sleep away!

div.stage: (Nemesis rises invisible behind Clytemnestra, L. C., and speaks through tremulo music)

sp.speaker: Nemes.
sp.l: Now is the time, all my resources rallying,
To pull the wires and set these puppets dallying,
Anticipate the tyrant's crime-earned woes,
And hasten matters to their fated close;
My mission I at once will set about,
True men come by their own when knaves fall out.
Come, Jealousy—obedient to my will,
Thy subtle poison through her veins distil!

div.stage: (Nemesis sinks—Clytemnestra appears inoculated with a new feeling—she observes Ægisthus and Chrysothemis with distrust)

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: (aside) What are they saying? I'm inclined to think
A nod accompanied by such a wink
Means something!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: (receiving the bunch of violets from Chrysothemis) Are these violets for me?
You're not forgetful of the day I see.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Oh no, I found them nestling in their beds
This morning, and they raised their modest heads,
Blushing to find that I was up before 'em.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: (aside) Violets should blush which violate decorum.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: They are the prettiest that I could gather.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: (aside) Ogling! he's old enough to be her father!
(aloud) When you've quite done exchanging compliments,
Perhaps you'll explain this matchless impudence!
Flirting before my face.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: (astonished) Flirting? oh, aunt—

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: I can't imagine—

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: No, of course you can't,
You never can—

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Harm, aunt, I ne'er met any—

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: And I had no idea—

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: You haven't many.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: But I assure you—

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Yes, you'll soon the folly see,
Of such assurance with so little policy.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: (C., deprecating) My love.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Oh don't love me!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Your word is law,
I promise not to do so any more,
Though I don't yet quite see her crime's immensity.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Good evidence of your own heavy density!
And pray where is Electra?

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: In her room,
Weaving a chaplet for her father's tomb,
Content, she says, for happier times to wait,
And bend, in mute submission to her fate.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Bid her unbend herself and come here straight,
Such shameless conduct would a saint provoke.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: (aside) It won't touch you then.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: I only spoke.
Nothing's occurred to make you thus give way.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: That girl shall married be without delay.
Now, as I've family duties to attend to,
We'll this discussion put at once an end to.
You'll join the hunt.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: I hunting go?

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Of course.
I've taken care to order round your horse,
For idle men are always in the way at home.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: I'll be so quiet if you'll let me stay at home.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: You used to like the chase!—I see!—

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: The fact is,
Of late, my dear, I've got so out of practice
Since we've been married, long experience teaches
I've never worn, nor am to wear the breeches.

div.stage: The sound of horns. Enter Huntsmen and Retainers through centre arch from L. U. E.

sp.speaker: Huntsman
sp.l: Will't please your majesty to join the sport?
Your thoroughbred is saddled in the court
Champing his bit.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Oh! that is a decider,
For I am not a bit a champi'n rider;
The clouds are threatening too, and seem to say
Our marriage morn will prove a wettin' day
From which, excuse me, I'm induced to dread
A quartan ague from my thorough bred.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: No, go you must; your thoroughbred 'tis clear
Is needed to prevent your loafing here.
Why, Agamemnon rode! they'll say in scoff,
From him to you was a sad falling off.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: 'Twixt you and me, and probably my steed,
I feel there'll be a falling off indeed.
But here goes!

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Shrewdly answered,

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: You're too good,
With such a wife the husband must be shrew'd.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: The dinner hour for seven o'clock we fix,
So mind you don't return, at least, till six.

div.stage: Exit, L. 1 E.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Now since we've got our work cut out before us,
We'll make believe we like it in a chorus.

spGrp.head: Song and Chorus—Air, "Kiss me Quick and go, my Honey."

lg.l: A southerly wind and a cloudy sky
Prolaim a hunting morn,
The deadly breeches I must mount
I've not for seven years worn;
I ventured once to plead excuse,
She kicked me out of bed,
And while I struggled with my boots,
Now what do you think she said?
Oh cut your stick and go, my hubby,
Cut your stick and go;
Don't rub your eyes, but I advise
You cut your stick and go.
And now the royal hunt is up,
I must get up as—well,
And clamber up that thoroughbred
From which last time I fell;
I never can forget that day
They picked me up for dead—
And yet to-day I can't say nay,
You all heard what she said.
Then let's be quick and go, my honeys,
Let's be quick and go,
As't must be done, we'll call it fun,
So let's be quick and go.

spGrp.stage: Chorus repeated and exeunt, R. U. E.

div.head: Scene Second.—A Chamber in the Palace. Music—Air, "The Miller of the Dee," very slowly.
div.stage: Enter Electra, L., her hair dishevelled, her dress torn and disarranged, shoes unsandaled and down at heel.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Another day has passed, and yet another
Brings with it's light no tidings of my brother.
While poor Electra, wearied of expecting,
By all neglected, and herself neglecting,
Resembles much as classic heroine can
The well-known slip-shod, Good-for-Nothing Nan;
These locks of gold, when servants on me waited,
Used to be carefully electra-plaited,
Now all dis-sheffield down my shoulders flow
No friendly comb'll make them comb-il-faut;
Where a "deserted auburn" they remain,
I fear not "loveliest even of the plain."

div.stage: Enter Chrysothemis, R.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Oh, aunt's in such a temper!

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: In at last?
She has been out of it for some time past.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: And what I can have done I'm sure I'm not aware.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: What matter.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: (hesitating) Only—

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: (contemptuously) True, I had forgot you were
A little sycophant!

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: I am, I vow,
More than a little sick of aunt just now.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: If then you don't her indignation fear,
Enlist in my cause as a volunteer.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Join a forlorn hope? No, I thank you dear,
When I my own light company can choose,
Pray, why should I exchange into the blues?
No, a fast life for me! "Laugh while you may"
Has ever been my motto.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Have your way,
But you mistake to call a gay life fast,
That must be slow, that's without trouble passed.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Here comes my aunt? I'd best retire, since she
Has taken an ant-ipathy to me.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Where's all that courage that you talked about?
Meet her at once, and boldly face it out.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Meet her? a lighted candle you might as
Well introduce to an escape of gas!
There'll be a blow up if we meet—discreeter
'Twill be to turn myself off, at the meet-her!

div.stage: Exit, R.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: So, all desert me!
(coldly to Clytemnestra) Pray may I solicit
The cause, ma'am, of this unexpected visit?

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Electra, you've your father much offended;

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: About my father, least said soonest mended;

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Oh, you allude to fables long refuted.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: It was, ma'am, to all—you—did I all-u-ded,

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: My own child! must I lectured be by her?

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: I am Electra! not a lecturer.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Besides, what's done is done—

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: That's very true,
But much that's not done, yet remains to do.
Then let Ægisthus triumph while he may,
Work his own will, and exercise his sway,
Till the gods, pitying this distracted land,
Summon Orestes to arrest his hand.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Your brother? Sure you've heard the news? he's dead, so
Will never trouble us—

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: It has been said so!
Yet cannot I forget a certain oracle—

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Asserting an untruth, for, from his curricle
Which threw him out, a lifeless corse he fell,
Throwing out, o' course, the prophecy as well ;
Meantime, what ails you, that you needs must rove,
Despite our orders, to the cypress grove!
Pluck my choice flowers into wreaths to twine,
And spill, while in the wood, our bottled wine ?

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: 'Twas a libation,

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Yes, but you forget
You took the claret from the cellaret
To waste upon these empty demonstrations,
I've scarcely patience with your scarce libations.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: It was not I—so that reproach may spare it—
Who was the first to tap my father's claret.
Have you no tributes to bestow? I pity you.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: I wish you'd try boots, for your shoes don't fit you.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: E'en in my shoes my sympathy's revealed
With him whose soul you sent down unan-healed.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Still the old tune and words!

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: 'Twill be the same,
Until Orestes shall his birthright claim,
Then will I change my note, and sing, I swear,
A different tune, in fact, the rightful heir !
Now I'll a walk take, this dispute to end,
And seek the change of air you recommend.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Was ever queen plagued with a child like this?
I may say two, for there's Chrysothemis;
Henceforth I shall enjoy no peace of mind
Until I see her marriage contract signed,
So will for Lycus send, without delay.
(to Electra) I've no more time to waste on you.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Good day!

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: And where is he for whom so long I've striven?
Would I could be assured he's even living!
Kind Destiny, his guardian to the last,
Watch o'er him on what shore soever cast,
And, Fortune, though disaster strive to floor him,
Rest o'er his arms till you to mine restore him!

lg.l: Oh! brother, would I knew, dear,
Where 'tis you roam;
They do not tell me true, dear,
Who say you'll ne'er come home.
I'm sure the cruel fate
Which makes their hearts rejoice
Can ne'er have overtaken you,
For there's a still small voice
Whispering solace to my heart
To dispel its midnight gloom!
Orestes, we have missed you,
Pr'ythee, hasten home.
My dreams are all about you,
For all the hopes I rear
Of vengeance, are, without you
Quite desperate, I fear.
Patient I wait and watch,
Cheered by that hope's faint ray
You'll homeward turn your footsteps
And wipe my tears away,
For my efforts are in vain
While you delay to come,
Orestes, I have missed you,
Hasten—hasten home!

div.stage: Exit, R.

div.head: Scene Third. —The sacred Grove of Cypress, through which runs a path supposed to lead to the Tomb of Agamemnon; open country, R.
div.stage: Enter Orestes and Pylades, L., the former bearing a cinerary urn.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Thus far into the bowels of the land,
A process only miners understand—
Have we marched on. Behind us Argos lies.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: To see it one must needs have Argus eyes.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Close here—Mycenæ. (pointing, R.)

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Then you tread the earth
Once more of the fair land that gave you birth.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: True, but I can't much gratitude evince,
I've given it such a wide berth ever since,
Nor would I venture now, but for the rumour
That I am dead—we'll that delusion humour;
Indeed, to make maternal instinct duller,
I'll swear I died myself to give it colour.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: What! at your own death be the undertaker?
But there's your mother, can you hope to make her
Deaf to the voice of nature?

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: There's no danger,
For seven years I've play'd the Son and Stranger,
And luckily, this cinerary urn
Supposed my ashes to contain, will turn
Suspicion from my person :—once we've gained
Credence, and footing in the house obtained,
We then may stand at ease, or I shall, rather,
Move one step nearer to remove one step-father,
Who in the downfall of our house will glory,
First floor'd by our one ready-furnish'd story.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: But should he doubt the urn, and perhaps begin to
Think it a case that should be well look'd into,
He, our returns will smoke, and truly say
'Tis mere sham dust and not your genuine clay;
The plot's found out by but the cover lifting,
For yours are ashes that will not bear sifting.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: He'll never go to see—how can he, pray,
While we contrive to keep him at Urn Bay.

spGrp.head: Song, Orestes.—Air, "Oft in the Stilly Night."

lg.l: Soft if not silly quite
You must I fear have found me,
If you think I can't bring off right
The troubles that surround me.
Dispel your fears my boyhood's years
My manhood will betoken,
Or that they'll learn aught from the urn
Which will remain unbroken.
Soft if not silly, &c.
I shall remember all
The lies we have link'd together—
When I recount my fall,
I doubt most shrewdly whether
They'll take to task, or think to ask
The how, or when, or wherefore,
Quite satisfied that I have died,
The only fact they care for.
Soft if not silly, &c.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: (looking off, R.) But who comes here, with votive offerings laden ?

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: (with indifference) Some pious peasant.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: No—a glorious maiden !
What dignity and grace in every movement,
Although her costume might bear some improvement:
In mien a princess, though apparelled humbly.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: I see, she's coming—I don't see she's comely.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: That taper waist!

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: (staying him) Yes—taper's a good name;
Don't burn your fingers at that taper's flame.

div.stage: (becomes interested as he recognizes his sister Electra advancing)

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Stay! (clutching the arm of Pylades)

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Hey!

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Aye!

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Why?

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Oh!

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: It cannot be!
That form! yes—I am not deceived! 'Tis she.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: No doubt I shall agree to all you've stated,
If you will take the trouble to translate it.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: My sister—yet I mustn't yet embrace her!

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: I'll act as proxy for you.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: I dare say, sir.
If to the good cause loyal she remain
As yet we know not, so, to ascertain
Rehearse our story of the urn, my friend,
And coil a tail about my hapless end;
While I, to make her disposition clear,
Conceal myself, and thus get a hide—here.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Sure, with an empty jar you would not mock her?

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Not being a laden jar it need not shock her!

div.stage: They retire, L. U. E.
Enter Electra, R. U. E., bearing votive offerings for the tomb.

lg.l: I've the matter fairly pondered,
And its many pathways seen,
But I scarcely know which road leads
To the vengeance that I mean.
For what can a lonely maiden,
With a task that brimming o'er
With difficulty do, but ask
For her brother, and nothing more?
With no advice to guide me,
I must still go blundering on,
Till I fear the hour for action,
Long arrived will soon be gone.
Let me hear the welcome music
Of his footfall on the floor—
'Tis surely not too much to ask
Only this, and nothing more.
Thus for weeks and months I'm brooding
O'er hopes too long deferred;
Orestes promised to return,
I know he'll keep his word,
Could I but see him face to face
With his worthless pa-in-law—
That party would like nothing less,
And I'll ask nothing more.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: (kneels, c.) Ye gods who rule the destinies of kings,
Look down upon this dreadful state of things!
If for misdeeds ye retribution purpose,
Let fall your lightning on these proud usurpers.
Our country groans, so ruthlessly they bleed her;
While the inhabitants, without a leader,
Stir not to staunch her wounds! — there's not a man
Will be the spirited leader of the van;
Though factious citizens in gloomy knots,
Sit as hens brooding o'er their half-hatched plots;
E'en knowing blades with hunger, through the town
Become sharp set, for taxes grind them down.
Lycean Phœbus, (kneels) make these patriots bolder,
The rebel fires which in each bosom smoulder,
Into a blazing conflagration fan,
And send me, I implore thee!—a young man.
sp.stage: (observing Pylades, who approaches, L. C., bearing the urn)
sp.l: (aside) Good looking, too—and I in such confusion!

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Pardon this unintentional intrusion,
Fair lady, and be sure I no offence meant.
(aside) That's pretty well, I think, for a commencement,
(aloud) I'm to Mycenæ bound, where they expect me.
But fear I've missed the path—can you direct me?

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: (pointing, R.) This spot a plain view of the city yields;
There is a nearer path across the fields, —
You'll have to ford a brook, through, by that way,
But if you can't afford, nor brook delay,
You'll find the distance will by half be shortened.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Thanks, ma'am, the news I bear is most important,
From Strophius, King of Phocis.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Ha! I presage
The worst news of Orestes in that message;
Speak—and allay an anxious sister's fears.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Alas, I can but answer with my tears;
My assistance, like a cistern 's full of water!
But if you be great Agamemnon's daughter,
You'll mutely bear this new affliction.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Who
Can be at once a mute and bearer, too?
But come, the sad particulars disclose.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: 'Tis pity—but I promised, and here goes :

lg.l: It was a sad affair that befel that smart young man,—
Not a maid but stole a glance at him as through the lists he ran,
With his harness light and horses bright, and garbed as choicest taste equipped 'em,
He took the lead and kept it too, so swiftly round the course he whipp'd 'em.
Crack went the lash, ri, tol, &c.
But turning round to take a look what made his rivals lag,
His horses made a sudden swerve, and touched the turning flag;
Then like a rocket from the shock (such cruel grief the gods can send us),
He spun up there into the air, and came down a most tremendous
Whack on his back, fol lol, &c.
It was a sad reverse the most impartial will declare,
For the right heir unto the throne to be thrown right unto the air,
But so it was, and all because he would not keep his eyes before him,
He fell a corse upon the course, from which home of course they bore him,
Back in a sack, fol, lol, &c.
For your better understanding, I must tell you that the Phocians
About the mode of burial have most eccentric notions ;—
His ashes burned, were then inurned, for into this funeral vase I swept 'em,
And thinking as his sister, you might like to see 'em, kept 'em.
Packed, fol, lol, &c.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: This vessel, then?

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: (aside) I of the trick repent—
(aloud) The man you mean is in this monument!
Although in this form you might not have known him
But as de mortuis nil nisi bone-um
I as his best friend for his dust contracted,
And in this urn hermetically packed it!

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Alas! I was prepared for this, because
I knew Orestes had been in the vars.
Let me look on the sad memorial, pray—
Fie—a tea-urn.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Do not t—urn away,
Not having time the matter to discuss,
A tea urn seemed a fit sar—coffee—gus.
Besides, the mode of burial I thought a—
Ppropriate, for one so often in hot water!
And so to soothe a sister's pious yearnings,
I have saved up all your brother's little urnings.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Kind thoughtful friend, I pray you give it me,
Let me embrace the vase that once vas he.
And what you ask, I promise without fail!

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: An urn's a steam vessel, not meant for sale,
Take it, and welcome.

div.stage: (gives it to her and retires up to Orestes)

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: How old feelings rush up,
And to my eyes unbidden fountains gush up!
I as 'twere yesterday remember well
What miseries his infancy befel,
The painful cutting of his earliest tooth,
And other incidental to his youth,
This urn appropriately suggesting three things.
His infant cough, hiccups, and baby teethings.
More clearly still back on my memory flow
The souvenirs of seven years ago.
When I from tyrants' menaces to snatch him,
Sent him abroad, for fear they should dispatch him?
And thought a tardy vengeance to enjoy,
Bringing my hopes to anchor round that boy,
Now since harsh fate removes the channel's mark,
All my small craft must founder in the dark.

div.stage: (Orestes rushes to her from his concealment, R. U. E.)

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: (c.) Not so, dear sister.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Pray who are you, sir?

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: I'd but one brother.
Can't you then infer?

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: 'Tis hard, this contradiction as I view it
To reconcile.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: I reckons I'll soon do it.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: It is — it is'nt! Yet that well known voice.
Yes—no.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: You have the privilege of choice.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Orestes! (throws herself into his arms)

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Oh, rest easy on that head,
In spite of all this gentleman has said
Upon my word and honour I'm not dead;
But for a further proof my tale is true—
Observe my linen.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Marked Orestes, too!

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Well, never mind the number.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Oh! my brother.
Even without these proofs 'twere hard to smother
The inward voice that whispers your recovery.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: True, 'tis the invoice marks the goods delivery.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: But, why deceive me?

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: I apologize;
That dust was meant to throw in other eyes,
Though first we tried its influence on you,
To find you, as we reckon'd, staunch and true;
But, since you seem to stand, like strangers ill at ease,
I'll introduce you—there—my sister—Pylades,
Our trusty colleague.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: (to Electra) Put me to the proof
I'll think no feat too great in your behoof.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Now what's the news at home? Have they been starving you?
You look so ill—and who's this upstart parvenu
So unlike our own Agamemnon ?

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: True.
He's very different from the Pa ve knew,
But I must own, although they treat me vilely
From morn to night I'm rated very highly,
While prying eyes all secresy deny us,
Making the court a court of nice eye pry us.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Let vengeance which has long lain dormant, burn in
My breast! Its a long lane that has no turning.
So now en route and forward as we trudge it,
You can unfold the rest of the home budget.

div.stage: (a bugle sounds distant, L. U. E.)

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: A horn! the hunting party! I doubt whether
It will be prudent we be seen together.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: You're right—if to the palace you precede us,
We will be up and doing when you need us.

div.stage: Exit Electra, R.
(Orestes and Pylades retire a little, R., looking after Electra—Ægisthus enters, L. U. E., through the thicket—he is habited in the costume of the chase, torn, wet and dirty—he sounds a horn)

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Amid those branches I have lost my route,
I play a trump, but no one follows suit!

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: (advancing, R.) May we enquire, sir, what dis—aster's fretting you?

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: (c.) Oh, gentlemen, I've lost my way, my horse, my retinue!
(sounds horn) In vain I blow—the birds, with echoing throats
Alone will take up my dishonoured notes.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: (L.) Birds? Fast men blow the post-horn for a lark.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: That is a horni—tho'—logical remark,
But don't apply to my case, for in me
You an unhappy hunting party see.
"A southerly wind and cloudy sky proclaim
A hunting morning"—and so, out we came :
We reached the park—the hounds threw off, of course,
A movement which was followed by my horse.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: You were unhorsed!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: The animal was vicious;
Indeed, the whole day has been unhorse—spicious!
On flew the hounds, and yelping through the park,
Left me a tarrier—with a loss of bark.
I, while the others kept their seats in clover,
Was such a green that I was grazed all over.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: They left you in the slough of despond here?

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Worse—it was in the slough of that pond there;
A situation I did not desire—
You see there's no occasion to add—mire !
sp.stage: (turns round and shows himself covered with mud)
sp.l: Galled by the saddle, sadly I remained
In water, that was not as I was—strained.
Fearing a ditch additional to meet,
Where I might my Graze Elegy repeat;
Till finding mine a sinking situation,
Like a great man, I rose with the occasion,
Went wandering on amid these tangled trees,
Until I thought wanders would never cease!

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: If you're fat-igued, on us you'd better lean.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: We'll be your guides, though doubtless when you're seen
By the street boys, you'll find you're guyed enough;
For they'll provide the stares——and show you up.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Thanks, friends; but first your names I fain would learn.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: You'll give us your address, sir, in return?

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Of course—my costume so to seed has run,
I'd gladly change address with any one.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: I am the king, ha! ha! who got a fling, ha! ha!
Over a thing, ha! ha! they call a Ha! Ha!

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: He is the king, ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: 'Tis an odd thing, ha! ha! fate should thus bring, ha! ha! us together, ha! ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: While here we must amuse you, ha! ha! to the queen to introduce you, ha! ha! I shall be proud, ha! ha! if I'm allowed, Ha! ha! which I much doubt, ha! ha! entres nous, but ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Pylad. | Orestes.
sp.l: We shall be proud, ha! ha! if honoured so far, ha! ha!
But, sire, this condescension.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Ha! ha! the matter pray don't mention.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: If he's your new papa, fate lends her aid so far.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: If he's my new papa, fate lends her aid so far.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Home you must come, ha! ha! you and your chum, ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: I need not go far for vengeance, ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: You need not go far for vengeance, ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: She may look glum, ha! ha! no matter, ha! ha!

div.stage: Exit Ægisthus, supported by Orestes and Pylades, R. U. E.

div.head: Scene Fourth. —The Curtained Gallery.
div.stage: Enter Chrysothemis, R.

sp.speaker: Chrysothemis
sp.l: Orestes is returned! What joy! Yet he
May long ere this have quite forgotten me!
Does he still wear my portrait next his heart
With which he promised he would never part?
"Give me," said he, "your miniature, I pray,
To look on every minute you're away."
But did he mean it sure? or was the intent
Naught better than an empty compliment;
One of those bubbles men with soft soap blow
To please a woman's fancy, who, below,
Delighted sees the fairy globe mount higher,
Then like a dream, break, vanish, and expire?
Nay, I'll not think it —'twill not do to be
So hard on one who was so soft on me.
Here comes my aunt, and Lycus in her train,
To try his second-hand suit on again;—
'Twas but this morn she for my coldness chid me;
I wish he'd run away with aunt, and rid me
Of both at once; but 'tis too much to hope
To merge the two bores in one aunt elope!

div.stage: Enter Clytemnestra with Lycus, who appears anxious to escape, L.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Come in! What do you fear?

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: 'Twas but this morn
That she turned up her nose at me in scorn,
And though she didn't in plain terms refuse, she
Distinctly meant nay by her ney-retrousseé;
While, singular but sympathetic fact,
My nose became disjointed by the act;
When love's in question, as you may suppose,
The man's ears aint soothed by the lady's noes,
So please, I'll call again this day six months.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: No—if 'tis done, it must be done at once;
I'll send her to you, and remember "Faint
Heart ne'er, &c."—in bright colors paint
The joys that to a wedded life belong.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: I can't paint well, but I can pitch it strong.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Wait while of your arrival I inform her!
And should she still continue cold, I'll warm her.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: I'll to the sticking place my courage screw,
And brace my nerves up for the interview.

spGrp.head: Air, "Would she but name the day," —"Satanella."

sp.l: Oh, would she but name the day,
Or let me mention it for her;
If she would only say,
Sweetheart, I am yours to-morrow!
Why does she floor me so;
Vex me with long delay?
Leave me to sigh, heigho!
Why can't she name the day?

spGrp.stage: (makes great exertions to reach a very high note—Chrysothemis runs in, R., in feigned alarm)

sp.speaker: Chrysothemis
sp.l: What's happened? Dear, sir, are you in much pain?
You've over-reached yourself, I fear, to gain
A high note, and are suffering from the strain;
Still in my ears that piteous wail is ringing.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: (offended) What you call piteous wailing, I call singing.
And there are many, tho' I may do badly,
Who'd give their ears to sing as well, miss, gladly!

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Their ears! that sacrifice would not much cost them,
They'd like your music better when they'd lost them.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Oh, why thus jeer a heart's pure fond desire?
You know 'tis dangerous to play with fire.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: This morn I threw cold water on your suit,
Enough to deluge you from head to foot,
And put out every spark you else might nurturè,
Unless your suit were made of gutta percha.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Put me to any water proof you will,
So I get a perch here in your heart still.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: You've had your answer, why thus persevere ?
If some one I could name were only here,
And saw you teaze me, he'd occasion seize
To right me properly and cross your teaze.
If he the down-strokes of his round hand tries——

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: He'd cross my teaze by dotting both my eyes:
I understand—a system taught by Smart.
And who's this happy sharer of your heart?

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: How foolish! his suspicion I've incurred.
'Tis nobody.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Nobody? On my word,
I wish that I were nobody.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Ne'er fear, it
May come in time, you are so very near it.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Madam! But, I'll my indignation swallow
Though it should choke me.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Nay, that doesn't follow;
Your indignation has so little menace in't,
You couldn't swallow anything more innocent.

div.stage: Enter Clytemnestra, R.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Well, is it settled ?

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Yes; I think it's settled.
Your majesty, the belle is too high mettled
To chime in, as she's told with anything,
Although she seems quite clear about the ring.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Why how's this? do you dare dispute my will?

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: No, aunt, if you'll, by way of codicil,
Let me choose whom I like and whom refuse.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Well, but time presses and we've none to lose;
To keep relations friendly I but see
In this mate here material guarantee.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Your kindly project I've no wish to baffle,
Hadn't you better put me up to raffle?
A prize to wrestle for? (aside) A good idea,
'Twill make the intentions of Orestes clear.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Agreed and to make sure the contest's fair
To all, it shall be done upon the square,
The public square, I mean, amid the games.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: If none appear to urge his prior claims,
I'll make my mind up to the worst,— that's you,
Or any one in short, I don't care who.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Excuse me, madam, wrestling is an art
Which of my youthful studies formed no part,
Besides I'm delicate about the shins,
And not so firm as might be on my pins,
While shoes that pinch me, prudently admonish
That I am for a wrestler much too Cornish.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: You run no risk, for, without my permission
No one will dare appear in opposition.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Under those circumstances I'll away
And brace my sinews for the manly fray.!

div.stage: Enter Ægisthus dressed as in Scene I., with Pylades bearing the urn, L.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: My dear, may I make bold to introduce
An interesting stranger?

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: What's the use
Of bringing home, to make our larder thinner
Guests, when I'm not prepared to stand a dinner,
E'en on the cheap plan that the Times would bring
In vogue?

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: He's good news.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: That's another thing.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Mentions your poor boy's death.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Then every dish
Is his, if only the desert I wish
Has fallen on Orestes! (to Pylades) Sir, you're welcome—
My niece—(introduces him to Chrysothemis)
you have some piteous news to tell? Come
I know its purport, out with it, don't spare it,
Besides I am strong-minded, and can bear it.

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: To coil it up then,
in the smallest space,
Your son was entered for a chariot race
The goal is near—a pillar intervenes,
Smashing the chariot all to smithereens !

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: I see he shaved the post too closely, where—
Too close a shave cut off his father's heir !

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Excuse a mother's feelings—the essentials
You've mentioned—may I ask for your credentials?

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: That Death the 'graver has struck off the prince—
This proof before all letters will convince.
Be satisfied—Orestes is not far.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: To a mother's feelings this is a sad jar.
Remove the mournful evidence, I pray,
sp.stage: (to Lady, who exits with urn, L.)
sp.l: I've no time to cry over it to-day.
The games require our presence.
sp.stage: (all move, L., as if going off)

div.stage: Enter Electra, R., she is handsomely dressed—her hair neatly arranged, and her manner joyous.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: What, mamma!
Going without me?

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Why, how changed you are!
This, for the ill-conditioned sloven miss
An unexpected metamorphose is.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: True, dear—I, under favour be it said,
Ne'er met a more fast metamorphosed maid!
I fear I must be wandering in my mind.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: You'll not stray far the space is too confined.
Why, you are quite finely tricked out !

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Yes, and you
Will soon find you are finely tricked out too!

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: That flush of pleasure and joy-lighted eye,
Explain and say, my pretty coz—'cos why?

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: My daughter, sir. (introduces Electra to Pylades)

sp.speaker: Pylad.
sp.l: Lady, I kiss your hand.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: He does it too! Ah, now
I understand
Her change of dress—'tis easy to infer,
These happy tidings must have tidy-ed her.
With that young man too she's in love, I see,
Which to those well oiled locks supplies the key.

sp.speaker: Ægis.
sp.l: Let us sad thoughts of past times chase away,
And mingle with the pastimes of to-day.
While that we have no false pride to attest,
Chrysothemis shall foot it with the rest.

spGrp.head: Quintette—Aegisthus, Clytemnestra, Electra, Pylades, Chrysothemis, —Air, "Girl, I left behind me."

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: The sports begun—let's see the fun,
Front places are bespoken;
What sight is there that can compare
With seeing heads well broken ?

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: Young Lycus waits to lead the fêtes,
Then let's be off to find him;
Twill cheer his eyes to see his prize—
The girl he left behind him!

sp.speaker: Ægist.|Clytem.
sp.l: } Young Lycus, &c.

sp.speaker: Electra.|Chryso.
sp.l: I hope his pate may meet the fate
To which our prayers consigned him,
Before he tried to win as bride,
The girl he left behind him.

div.head: Scene Fifth.— The Great Square of the City during the Fête.
div.stage: The Stage is crowded with People engaged in various pursuits—Some are looking at the exhibition of a classical "Punch and Judy," R. C.; some are endeavouring to obtain wreath of laurel from the head of a greasy pole, c.; others are engaged witnessing the performance of a Strolling Company of Actors on a Thespian cart, L.; Two Players engaged in a contest, their partizans looking on encouraging them, R. The Scene opens to
A Ballet Divertissement!
Enter Philario, R. U. E.

sp.speaker: Philar.
sp.l: Their majesties approach! and bid me say,
They give you leave for this once to display
The loyalty which fills your hearts, no doubt,
In one prolonged enthusiastic shout!
You seem inclined to take your time, I see;
Perhaps you'd better take your time from me.
Now, hip-hip-hip-Hurrah!
I was to add, if anybody feel
A diffidence in answering this appeal
With heart and voice, 'tis possible, instead,
That gentleman will answer with his head.
Take my advice, then, or you may repent it,
Immediately be joyous and contented;
Let your enthusiasm over bile,
And mind you smile as you were wont to smile!

div.stage: Grand March—Enter The Royal Party, Ægisthus, Clytemnestra, Lycus in the costume of an Athlete, with a cloak thrown over him; Chrysothemis, Electra, and Pylades enter R. U. E, and come down to L. At the instigation of Philario some of the People faintly say, "Hurrah," in desponding unjoyous tones.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Thanks, friends, this genuine unbought applause
Speaks volumes for the wisdom of our laws!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Whoever "oh's" will find he has to pay!
I did not catch that last remark.

sp.speaker: People.
sp.l: Hooray!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Yes, these spontaneous outbursts of affection
Are pleasant matter for a king's reflection.
Pshaw! this is weakness!
Doubtless you all know
We are about our fair niece to bestow
On the best wrestler, who, you'll understand,
Must carry off the palm to win her hand ;—
But that you may all learn the stakes imperilled,
We publish full particulars in the Herald.

div.stage: A Herald advances, c., while a roped arena is formed round him.

sp.speaker: Herald.
sp.l: Oh, yes! oh, yes! which means, oh, know you all
'Tis my vocation to the lists to call
Whoever ventures to pick up the glove
Thrown down by Lycus for his lady love!
Lycus, the Argos Gilliflower famous!

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Oh, dear! should any not an ignoramus
Appear, I'm floored!

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: On that head have no fear,
Against my champion none will dare appear;
Keep up your spirits.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Thanks—on that condition
My pecker holds its usual high position.

sp.speaker: Herald.
sp.l: Three times I sound my trumpet! (sounds—a pause) No reply?
sp.stage: (Lycus throws off his cloak and advances boastfully)

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: When once I stripped, I thought they would be shy!
Manner and style like mine not many men
Possess!—perhaps you'd better sound again.
They're much too deep for soundings, and they may
Take it as sound advice to keep away.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: With dread forebodings my sad mind oppressed is:
Alas! my only hope was in Orestes.
Why did I to this silly wager yield,
In full assurance he would take the field?
But he deserts me—

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Fye, you mustn't say so
All is not lost yet—prythee, don't give way so.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: And must I be that empty coxcomb's bride?

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: You shan't be tied to him whate'er be-tide:
Let me entreat you to be pacified?

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Be pacified? The troubles that arise,
Could ne'er have come to pass—if—I'd been wise.

sp.speaker: Herald.
sp.l: None enters an appearance, sir; —all mute.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Then mine will be an undefended suit.
Wake all the town, and let the people know it
Is the last time of asking. Go it—blow it!

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: That last blow is a last blow to my hopes.

sp.speaker: Ægis.
sp.l: No one will venture then within the ropes ?

div.stage: Orestes enters hurriedly, L. U. E., and makes his way through the Crowd.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: I will, sire, if it's all the same to you.

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: 'Tis he! 'Tis he!

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Hush! List to my imploring,
Two more such 'Tis he's will make up our floorin.'

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: 'Tis well! it matters little to my plan,
So she be married, who's the happy man.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: How could you think I would forsake you, dear,
When 'tis for sake of you that I am here?
'There is my gage, although I risk, I know,
A par-a-dise upon a single throw!

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: How very awkward! (to Orestes with assumed superiority) Are you used to falling?

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Wrestling with fate long time has been my calling
And in my college days I learned the charms
Of a good long pull at the Wrestler's Arms.

sp.speaker: Ægis.
sp.l: We'll put you to the proof; so, clear the ring,
And let them trip each other's heal and fling.
You shall try but one fall.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: Be that agreed.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: Now when you're ready, sir—

spGrp.head: Song. Air, "Come into the garden, Maud."

sp.l: Come into the ring, my lord,
Since down your gage is thrown;
Come into the ring, my lord,
Though I'm not in fit state I'll own—
In condition first-rate I'll own.
But your wordy challenge is wafted abroad,
And the trumpet defiance has blown,
For our breeze of this morning proves,
And the plan it our love it will try,
'Twere sinning to faint in her sight whom one loves,
Or instead—like a duffer—fight shy.
It aint in the light of a man she loves,
She'll look on whoever says die.
Come into the ring, my lord,
Since down your gage is thrown;
One of us will soon be floored,
And the lady the victor's own!

sp.speaker: One Of The Crowd.
sp.l: Well thrown, indeed.
sp.stage: (All the Crowd, "Hoo———!"—they are going to shout, but are stopped by the King)

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: How do you feel?—I'm not warm at all.
So if you'd like to try another fall,
We'll go "best out of three."

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: You're very kind.
To come off second-best out of one, I find
Is quite enough to put me out of breath,
Best out of three to me were sudden death!
sp.stage: (goes up to Queen—Boys take up ring)

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.stage: (rising and coming down, R., to Orestes)
sp.l: Since then your match her match with Lycus breaks,
I can't do less than offer you the stakes.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: An offer that's so handsome on its face
I need, sire, no caressing to embrace.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: The girl's at last disposed of that's a blessing!
sp.stage: (coming down, R. of King—Lycus, R. corner)
sp.l: Since the engagement seems so very pressing,
We'll set at once about the preparations;
Meantime accept my best congratulations.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: And mine.

sp.speaker: Lycus.
sp.l: And mine—for I don't see the fun
Of breaking several ribs in gaining one.
I pitched upon my head—

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: That's no hard case,
You couldn't pitch upon a softer place.
Stay! we must know the title of the winner.

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: You shall be satisfied, sire, after dinner.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: On to the banquet then, and after all
Your yarn is spun, we'll wind up in a ball!

div.stage: March.—Exeunt Ægisthus, &c., &c. R. U. E.—shouts and resumption of the music, and the Scene closes as the People go up the stage.

div.head: Scene Sixth. — Ante-chamber in the Palace.
div.stage: Enter Nemesis, C.

sp.speaker: Nemesis.
sp.l: So far, so well; but much is yet to do.
I really cannot tell if all of you
Recall the old Greek rule of stage propriety—
Which was the audience having had satiety
Of crime displayed and vengeance on it willed,
Upon the stage the actors were not killed,
But by some fanciful poetic means
Were decently disposed of— off the scenes!
Let none think we the grand old works despise,
Which for your modern eyes we modernize;
Since old Mycenae then, my scenic art
Displays—though you'll not find my scene a cart
As in those days—we'll not in this depart
From the old rule. So, though the guilty wife
And husband both are doomed to end their life
By changing poisoned cups, we'll leave the fumes
To work upon them in their dressing rooms
Behind the curtain. You'll enquire no doubt
How this catastrophe is brought about.
Learn then the queen has fixed her admiration
On Pylades, who, at my instigation,
Appears to listen to her overtures,
(While poor Electra all the pangs endures
Of Jealousy). Whereat, the queen her mind up
Has made, her former partnership to wind up—
Will dose the king's cup—the mode well she knows it,
For, in her case, experienta dose it.
Meantime, here comes the interesting victim,
Looking as though some sense of wrong had pricked him
To meditate revenge. Of both I'll spoil
The future hopes, while, from this mortal coil
Both simultaneously slip their cables,
And each on each with your leaves turn the tables.

div.stage: Enter Ægisthus, R.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: This cat-and-dog life can't go on much longer,
The cat has proved so very much the stronger.
Would that we lived in times some yet may see,
When married folks can separated be—
I could prove cruelty 'mongst other wee sins,
And sue for a divorce, for divorce reasons.
Meantime, some means I must use to get rid o' her
And start again in life a jolly widower—
Make up to — whom? Aye! there's the rub!

sp.speaker: Nemesis.
sp.l: Chrysothemis.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Chrysothemis? Why not? the notion's not amiss,
But there's a proverb not more trite than true,
Which treats about the old love and the new.
First, of the first dispose 'ere fix my choice on
A second—humph! what means to use though?

sp.speaker: Nemesis.
sp.l: Poison.

div.stage: Exit Nemesis, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: A good idea; yes, nothing can be clearer,
I'll drug her cup—South Attican Madeira—
'Tis fit for such a purpose I should choose
A wine that has no character to lose.
If she but take that draught, I am content
'Twill prove the rough draught of her settlement.
'Neath her nose—'neath her nose!
'Neath her nose at the banquet I'll manage to slip
A cup of South Attic Madeira,
With which if she ventures to moisten her lip,
She will not find her intellect clearer.
Where it grows—I suppose
Salt and senna may glow in the glass,
And rhubarb may crown the refection
So if but one drop to her palate may pass,
Though I scarcely conceive my fond wife such an ass,
She must pay for her strange predilection.
'Neath the rose—off she goes,
Without the least fear of detection!

div.stage: Enter Electra, R.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: A warning this to all unmarried maidens is
Who list to Cupid's too seductive cadences,
That fickle, perjured Pylades who swore to me
Such oaths as never mortal swore before to me,
Is flirting with the queen in the back garden!

div.stage: Enter Nemesis, L. 2 E.

sp.speaker: Nemesis.
sp.l: Be comforted, my child.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: I beg your pardon.
Are you aware, ma'am, these are private premises?

sp.speaker: Nemesis.
sp.l: No gates are strong enough to keep out Nemesis,
But to resume—your lover true remains,
'Tis but at my will he a passion feigns
For her.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: Can this be true ? or am I dreaming ?

sp.speaker: Nemesis.
sp.l: This new suit that you dread's made up of seeming,
When the work's done which I in hand have ta'en,
The seeming shall come all unstitched again.
The sword of Fate suspended
By justice over crime,
Waits only for my signal
To fall and now the time
Approaches—though deferred
The long account to close,
And give you at a word,
A triumph o'er your foes.
Cheer up, then,
For to-day, 'ere the sun has gone down,
For the past shall atone,
And you will own
You've more cause to smile than to frown.

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: I'll cheer up, ma'am,
And won't let my spirits go down,
For the kindness you've shown
I'll freely own, &c.

div.head: Scene Seven. — Grand Banquet Hall in the Palace —
div.stage: Guests seated at tables, which line the stage on either side—Ægisthus and Clytemnestra at a table on centre trap—Orestes and Chrysothemis at extremity of table, R.—Pylades, Electra, and Lycus, L.—Music.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: My friends, although of speeches from the throne
There are but few that kings can call their own,
By ministers contributed each particle,
I beg to say, mine is a genuine article :
The toast I now propose with loud acclaim,
Is the illustrious visitors who came
So lately to our Court,—drink we with zest
These two last copies of the Welcome Guest!
(aside) She's left her goblet in my reach—that's capital!
Hey, presto, pass!
sp.stage: (e exchanges his goblet for the Queen's, as he fancies, unobserved by her)

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: (aside)He's ta'en mine—ere he lap it all
Another sovereign on the cypress mount
Is carried forward to his long account.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Bumpers! (aside)Dear me, I fear there's something wrong,
This wine's so inconveniently strong;
One stoup's enough to make one stupid, quite.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: (aside)There is a taste in this that don't seem right.

div.stage: (cheers from all the Guests. Orestes rises to respond)

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: My friends, I thank you, and attention claim
While, as I promised, I divulge my name;
Learn my parental tree can boast a stem none
Inferior to that of Agamemnon. (sensation)
Concerning whom I could a tale unfold,
Whose lightest word would make your blood run cold,
And while it might your very breath suspend,
Makes me his particular heir to stand on end.
Hence your guest's name, as you've already guessed, is
Orestes, and your king.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Long live Orestes!

div.stage: (the King and Queen are yielding to the narcotic influence of the potions)

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: (dreamily)Of all this tumult what can be the reason?

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: It looks to me uncommonly like treason.

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: My son!

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: (advancing) Ah! that reminds me—now I'm warm,
I've an unpleasant duty to perform,
Imposed by fate. (draws)

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: Oh! spare yourself, my boy,
Ten minutes since I mention it with joy,
My poisoned cup was drank from by your mother!

sp.speaker: Clytem.
sp.l: I've but one consolation—you're another!

sp.speaker: Electra.
sp.l: For of yours let me tell you, every drop's
At least as deadly as cheap lollypops!

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: As many a victim, who, insanely willing
To have his likeness taken for a shilling,
Finds himself nothing like himself—so surely
I find, like him, I'm taken very poorly;
Both our cups drugg'd? It seems then I and you
Are both floored, and laid down with drug-it too!

sp.speaker: Chryso.
sp.l: Though I don't dote on aunty much, I vote
We do our best to get an anti-dote!

div.stage: Nemesis rises, C.

sp.speaker: Nemesis.
sp.l: Stir not! their time has come—leave them to me,
And let the Fates work out their own decree.
To you, Orestes, as of right belongs
(You the young martyr of a thousand wrongs,)
Mycenæ's throne, and on it, by your side
Chrysothemis shall sit, your well-won bride.
(to Electra) For you, whom snow, nor rain, nor taunt, nor gibe
Could drive from duty's path, I'll now prescribe;
Henceforth you'll shun those dangerous night draughts please,
To take, if I may say it, your pill-at-ease,
Resting in pillowed ease with Pylades.

sp.speaker: Ægist.
sp.l: I beg on this felicitous occasion,
To make the customary observation,
Bless you, my children! (to Nemesis) Thank you, ma'am, good-day.
(to Clytemnestra) My dear, I think our carriage stops the way.

div.stage: Ægisthus and Clytemnestra, with table, sink on C. trap

sp.speaker: Nemesis.
sp.l: Justice is done upon the guilty pair,
Yet, lest pollution hover in the air,
Tainting your future lives, these blood-stained halls,
Crime-clouded towers, and time-dishonored walls,
None here in their destruction to involve,
Must as a Polytechnic view, dissolve,
And like the baseless fabric of a vision,
Leave not a track to mark their old position!

div.stage: Nemesis waves her arm—the tables sink, and Scene breaks to pieces, or dissolves, revealing the last Scene

sp.speaker: Orestes.
sp.l: You've a power whose sway
The author must adore,
Bidding him decay
Or live a little more;
For in your verdict lies
The hope he has reared above
All others—or—he dies,
Such is your power—of glove!
Source of joy and woe,
Sealers of his fate,
Don't let him vanquished go,
Or quite repudiate
One who has known you well
As vulture less than dove—
None can better tell
Than he your power of glove!

div.stage: Nemesis. Chryso. Orest. Electra. Pylades. Lycus.
Curtain.
